newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr fatigued as rally effort frustrated.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr fatigued as rally effort frustrated.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished 1/2 cent poorer Monday and under threat of a fresh downtrend.
Enough bids did appear to rescue it from early lows but dealers cautioned their impact was exaggerated by a bank holiday in Sydney which made the market very illiquid.
Technically, the failure at 75 cents and resulting retreat through US$0.7400/20 support suggested its five month-old downtrend had further yet to run and put US$0.7310 at risk.
There was also a suspicion A$/US$ interest differentials could move further against it as local data disappointed while the U.S. economy continued to surprise with its strength.

By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency had steadied at US$0.7390/09 having inched up from an early US$0.7365 low, but remained well adrift of Friday's late US$0.7442/47 and last week's US$0.7505 high.
Traders said there were good bids lurking from chart support at US$0.7330 down to the 18-month low of US$0.7310 hit a couple of weeks ago, which should cushion the currency near term.

But chart watchers were not so sure it would hold this time and saw a risk of a new bear phase to US$0.7250 enroute to the 1995 low of US$0.7070. A recovery above US$0.7440 was needed to forestall the trend and atop US$0.7505 to signal a reversal.
Such a recovery would be hampered by lingering concerns lsat week's 50 basis point rate cut from the Reserve Bank was not, after all, the end of the year-long easing cycle.

Most analysts believed there was probably enough monetary stimulus in the pipeline -- 250 basis points off official rates and considerably more off mortgages -- to ensure an eventual pickup in economic growth .

But they conceded that with underlying inlfation expected to remain below the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target into next year and plenty of spare capacity in the economy, there was room to ease further should upcoming data disappoint.
And the data had certainly underwhelmed so far, with retail sales and building approvals last week both soft and the ANZ job advertisement measure today showing a sharp fall.

Job ads, usually regarded as a reliable leading indicator of employment growth, fell 2.9 percent in July after a downward revised 0.8 percent gain in June. Trend growth slowed to just 0.1 percent and analysts feared the poor result boded ill for the official labour data due on Thursday.
Median forecasts are for a 25,000 gain in jobs for July, up on the 11,900 recorded the month before -- but even then the two months together would not make up for May's 40,300 fall.
A weaker result, and particularly a drop in jobs, would stir talk of another easing and push money market rates yet lower.
The outlook contrasted with that in the U.S. where payrolls data Friday topped forecasts and a Purchasing Management survey on industry showed activity at a 2-1/2 year high.
The figures challenged the market's cosy assumption that growth was moderating naturally and another tightening from the Federal Reserve was not needed in the medium term, if at all.
The market responded by hacking 0.115 point off the December three-month Eurodollar contract to 94.110, implying a rate of 5.885 percent against the present 5.50 percent funds rate.
The corresponding Australian contract was at 95.08, implying a rate of 4.92 percent.
The RBA board holds its regular monthly meeting Tuesday, but since it had already had a secret meeting to agree on the rate cut, nothing much was expected to emerge from it.
The local currency was mixed on the crosses, being up at five year highs on the broadly weaker mark at 1.3778/93 from 1.3682/94 late Friday.
It lost ground on the yen to 87.47/57 from 88.52/62 and on the Kiwi at NZ$1.1476/01 from a firm NZ$1.1527/44 on Friday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
